Qualitative study (Grounded Theory, Symbolic Interactionism) with children aged 3-12 years with sickle cell anemia, a chronic condition causing recurrent pain. Explores children's experiences of pain, powerlessness, treatment, and family support. Meets all selection criteria: qualitative design, correct age range, chronic non-cancer pain condition, focuses on experiences and perceptions.

While the study involves young people (12-16 years) with sickle cell disease and mentions pain, the methodology is explicitly described as 'cross-sectional study using semistructured questionnaires' - this is primarily quantitative data collection, not qualitative research. Does not meet the qualitative research requirement.

Mixed-methods study with explicit qualitative results component. Involves adolescents with chronic pain and parents. Explores needs, experiences, and views regarding chronic pain management resources and services. Contains qualitative data about adolescent and parent perspectives on pain management. Conservative approach favors inclusion.

This is a classification/guideline document, not primary qualitative research. No children or families are studied; it describes a working group's development of ICD-11 chronic pain classification codes. Does not meet any selection criteria.

Qualitative study using photovoice (participatory qualitative method) with adolescents and young adults living with chronic pain. Includes focus group discussions exploring experiences, sources of joy, and peer support. Addresses how young people live with chronic pain and their perspectives. Meets selection criteria.

While qualitative and involving adolescents (11-17 years), the study focuses on Chronic Fatigue Syndrome/Myalgic Encephalomyelitis (CFS/ME), which is primarily characterized by fatigue rather than chronic pain. The review specifically targets chronic non-cancer pain conditions. Pain is not the primary focus of this study.

Qualitative study with adolescents post-kidney transplant, but the focus is on information needs throughout the transplant continuum. Pain is mentioned as one of four stressors but is not the primary focus. The study does not center on chronic pain experiences or pain management services.

Qualitative study (individual interviews, content analysis) with parent-adolescent dyads where adolescents have juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) or Crohn's disease. JIA is a chronic inflammatory condition with pain as a primary symptom. Explores treatment decision-making, quality of life considerations, and differing perspectives between parents and adolescents. Relevant to understanding family experiences with chronic pain conditions and treatment.

Qualitative study (semantic thematic analysis) with children aged 10-18 years, their parents, and healthcare providers. Specifically examines long-term pain experiences after major surgery, family experiences of pain, and barriers/facilitators to pain management interventions. Directly addresses chronic pain experiences and service perspectives.

Mixed-methods study with substantial qualitative component (semistructured interviews) with children aged 10-18 years with chronic pain at a tertiary pain clinic. Examines how children live with chronic pain, functioning limitations, and coping strategies. Identifies distinct patterns of adaptation. Highly relevant to review questions about living with chronic pain.

This is a Cochrane Review (systematic review of intervention effects), not primary qualitative research. The abstract indicates it assesses pharmacological treatment effects. Does not meet the qualitative research requirement.

Qualitative study (reflexive thematic analysis) with pediatric patients with chronic pain, parents, and healthcare professionals. Explores experiences with psychosocial aftercare following intensive pain treatment. Addresses treatment experiences, family perspectives, and service effectiveness. Directly relevant to review objectives.

Qualitative study (inductive reflexive thematic analysis) with youth aged 13-20 years with chronic pain and their parents. Explores lived experiences of managing chronic pain during the pandemic, access to care, coping strategies, and mental health impacts. Addresses how families live with chronic pain and experience services. Note: Age range slightly exceeds 18 but conservative approach favors inclusion.

Qualitative study about chronic non-cancer pain and opioid use, but the abstract does not specify that participants are children or adolescents. The study appears to be conducted at a general Pain Clinic without indication of pediatric focus. Cannot confirm the population meets the 3 months to 18 years criterion.

Qualitative participatory study (art workshops) with children aged 6-11 years with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), a chronic condition with pain as the most common symptom. Explores children's perspectives on symptoms, treatment side effects, and research priorities. Addresses children's views on their condition and treatment experiences.

This is a methodological guidance paper about meta-ethnography reporting standards, not primary qualitative research with children and families. No empirical data from children with chronic pain. Does not meet selection criteria.

While the study involves adolescents (12-18 years) with chronic pain and their families, the methodology is quantitative: 3-week pain diaries and questionnaires on quality of life. No qualitative data collection or analysis is described. Does not meet the qualitative research requirement.

Qualitative study with children (5-12 years) with cystic fibrosis, but CF is primarily a respiratory/genetic condition, not a chronic pain condition. The study focuses on religious/spiritual coping with illness generally, not specifically on pain experiences or pain management. Does not meet the chronic non-cancer pain focus.

Qualitative study with fathers of children with cystic fibrosis, but CF is not a chronic pain condition. The study focuses on emotional impact of caregiving, not on pain experiences or pain management. Does not meet the chronic non-cancer pain focus.

Qualitative study (interpretative phenomenological analysis) with youths aged 11-15 years with functional disorders and their parents. Functional disorders commonly present with chronic pain symptoms (e.g., functional abdominal pain, functional neurological disorders). Explores illness perceptions, healthcare experiences, and how families understand their condition. Relevant to understanding how children and families conceptualize chronic pain conditions.
